newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn bangs on EMU drum to drown out discord.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn bangs on EMU drum to drown out discord.

text.p: The Bonn government this week went out of its way to put across the message that everyone should stop worrying whether Germany will qualify for European monetary union.

Kicking off the week by gaining acceptance from European finance ministers for the final details of a German-proposed stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline in monetary union, official Germany continued to ride a wave of EMU optimism.
The torrent of renewed euro-phoria was unleashed by a pledge of commitment to EMU from the very top - direct from Chancellor Helmut Kohl himself.
Kohl gave Germany's EMU intentions a new lease of life by announcing last Thursday that he would stand for re-election in 1998 and linking this firmly to Europe's single currency plans.

Reaffirming Bonn's EMU commitment in Mannheim on April 4, Kohl said, "It is agreed that the stability criteria in the Maastricht treaty are not up for negotiation. Likewise the timetable for the common European currency must be observed.
"Current speculation over who will qualify for monetary union and whether Germany will meet the stability criteria is superfluous," he added.

Finance minister Theo Waigel, speaking in the town of Ludwigsburg on Thursday, gave similar reassurances. "Germany will fulfil the criteria. Even current developments give no cause to veer from these forecasts. But should there still be a need to act, we will not hesitate to do what is necessary."
On Friday, he told a meeting of his own political party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), "Germany will meet the criteria despite doubts from some corners."

And Finance Ministry secretary Juergen Stark stressed at a political meeting in Berlin on Thursday: "We shall meet the deficit criterion. There is no doubt about that...I don't know where this doubt is coming from."
But the uniform chorus of the official message was not loud enough to drown out niggling worries about Bonn's EMU plans.

Although the record employment numbers seen at the start of the year eased slightly in March, worries persisted as to whether Germany had any real hope of cutting last year's budget deficit of 3.8 percent back to a 2.9 percent target this year.

The target -- which compares the deficit to gross domestic product -- is only a whisker below the three percent level countries must meet to qualify for monetary union according to rules laid down in the 15-nation Maastricht Treaty.
Waigel, who has in the past insisted that that target means a deficit of 3.0 percent or less, spent the week avoiding comment on exactly what the Maastricht treaty required.

In Ludwigsburg, the text of his speech affirmed confidently, "I have not changed my view. I will oppose any weakening of the criteria, three is three... Convergence will determine the timetable -- for each country."
But when reading the speech, he dropped the phrases "three is three" and "convergence will determine the timetable".
He again avoided mentioning figures in Friday's speech.
And the six Bundesbank council members who commented on EMU in the past week presented anything other than a united front.

While some were confident of a punctual start -- particularly after an agreement this week on a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline within EMU -- others were doubtful of the nations' ability to meet the required economic targets.

Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister said in a speech in Frankfurt on Friday, "Many countries are finding difficulties in bringing their annual deficits under the level of three percent laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.
"There is still not sufficient certainty Germany will actually succeed," he added, saying he nonetheless expected a punctual start to EMU with a small group of members.
In a similar vein, council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said in Berlin on Thursday, "I am quite clearly opposed to any such attempt to start European currency union at any price."
He also mitigated against delaying the launch. "To me it is extremely questionable whether a postponement would lead to any improved (economic) convergence (between nations)," he said.

Yet council member Reimut Jochimsen argued that a delay should not be ruled out. "It is becoming increasingly evident, that Germany will find it extraordinarily difficult to meet the budget and debt criteria," he said.
"An EMU delay should not be categorically ruled out, turned into a taboo, or branded a question of war and peace."
And a fourth council member, Ernst Welteke, told German television it was simply too late for Germany to start a debate on the rationale of monetary union now.

"We cannot behave as though we are at the start of a debate. We agreed a Treaty of 15 countries... Many countries are taking the consequences and preparing for monetary union, while we are beginning a hectic debate about delay -- which is fuelled mostly by what I consider irrational arguments -- 20 months before the start," he said.
